stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Archival ledgers from an eighteenth-century silk workshop in Lyon name four master weavers, each of whom supervised a separate team at the drawlooms. The ______, most of them boys hired at the age of nine or ten, were responsible for lifting the heavy warp cords in the exact sequence that a pattern demanded.
explanation: The assistants belong to the weavers, so 'weavers' needs an apostrophe. The ledgers name four master weavers, so there are several owners, and a plural owner ending in s takes s'. The assistants own nothing; they are the subject of 'were responsible', so 'assistants' is a plain plural with no apostrophe. 'Weavers' assistants' has exactly that combination.

A.why: You saw that the weavers own the assistants but used the singular 's. The passage names four master weavers, so the owner is plural and needs s'.

C.why: You put the apostrophes on the wrong nouns. 'Weavers' is the owner and needs one. 'Assistants' is the subject of 'were' and owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe.

D.why: You got 'weavers'' right but added an apostrophe to 'assistants', which owns nothing. It is the plural subject of 'were responsible', and the interrupting phrase doesn't change that.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Of the eleven watersheds included in the Montana stream survey, only the Elk Fork drains an active glacier. The ______ therefore carry cold meltwater well into August, long after streams elsewhere in the survey have dropped to base flow and warmed enough to stress native trout.
explanation: The tributaries belong to the Elk Fork, which is a single watershed, so the owner takes 's. The tributaries own nothing. They are the subject of 'carry', so they take a plain plural with no apostrophe. That gives 'watershed's tributaries'.

A.why: The survey's eleven watersheds made you pick a plural owner. The sentence is only about the Elk Fork, though, so there is one owner and it needs 's, not s'.

B.why: You got the single owner right but added an apostrophe to 'tributaries'. That noun comes right before the verb 'carry' and owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe.

D.why: You put the apostrophe on the wrong noun. The watershed is the owner and needs 's. 'Tributary's' is singular and possessive, but the noun here is the plural subject of 'carry'.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Astronomers studying a binary system in the constellation Cygnus found that its two stars are nearly identical in size and brightness. Because the system's orbital plane lies almost edge-on to Earth, each star passes directly in front of the other once per orbit. The ______ produce two equal dips in the system's light curve every 41 days.
explanation: The eclipses belong to the two stars, so the owner is plural and takes s'. The eclipses own nothing. They are the subject of 'produce', so they take no apostrophe. That gives 'stars' eclipses'.

A.why: The singular 'system's' and 'each star' pulled you toward a single owner. The eclipses are made by both stars, so the owner is plural and needs s'.

B.why: You swapped the apostrophe's position. 'Stars' is the owner and needs an apostrophe. 'Eclipses' is the subject of 'produce' and owns nothing.

C.why: You got the plural owner right but also gave 'eclipses' an apostrophe. It sits right before the verb 'produce' and owns nothing.

stimulus: Producing a nineteenth-century Japanese woodblock print took several specialists. A designer drew the image, carvers cut it into cherry-wood blocks, and printers brushed on the ink by hand. The ______, stamped in the margin of every sheet, identified him as the man who had paid for the work.
explanation: The seals belong to the merchant, and the passage stresses that there was a single merchant, so the owner takes 's. The seals own nothing. They are the subject of 'identified', so 'seals' is a plain plural. That gives 'merchant's seals'.

B.why: The list of designers, carvers, and printers made you think of several owners. The text says the series was financed by a single merchant, and 'him' confirms there was one, so you need 's, not s'.

C.why: You moved the apostrophe onto the wrong noun. The merchant owns the seals and needs 's. 'Seals' is the plural subject of 'identified' and owns nothing.

D.why: You got the owner right but also gave 'seals' an apostrophe. 'Seals' owns nothing; it is the subject of 'identified'.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To study how fatigue affects pacing, sports scientists recorded every lap swum by the eighteen members of a single university swim club over one season of training. The ______ lap times, logged automatically by an underwater sensor system, showed that most athletes slowed sharply during the final quarter of long sets.
explanation: This blank has two owners in a row. The swimmers belong to the club, and there is only one club, so it takes 's. The lap times belong to the swimmers, and there are eighteen of them, so a plural owner takes s'. 'Lap times' then follows with no apostrophe. That gives 'club's swimmers''.

A.why: You got the swimmers right but made the club plural. The passage says a single university swim club, so it needs 's.

B.why: You got the club right but made the swimmers singular. The lap times belong to eighteen members, so 'swimmers' needs s', not 's.

C.why: You left the apostrophe off 'club', but the club owns the swimmers. Every noun that owns the next noun needs an apostrophe.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Ornithologist Inés Carvajal spent four summers tracking barn swallows from two colonies, one nesting beneath a highway overpass and the other in a dairy barn three kilometers away. Each bird carried a radio tag weighing less than half a gram. To Carvajal's surprise, the two ______ overlapped almost entirely, suggesting that birds from both sites were competing for the same flying insects over the same fields.
explanation: Check each noun in turn. The colonies own the foraging ranges, and the passage names two colonies ("the two"), so the owner is plural and ends in s: colonies'. The ranges don't own anything. They are the subject of "overlapped," so they are plain plural with no apostrophe. That gives "colonies' foraging ranges."

A.why: You were right that the colonies own the ranges, but you gave them a single owner with 's. The passage describes two colonies, and "the two" in front of the blank needs a plural noun.

C.why: You moved the apostrophe to the wrong noun. The colonies are the owners and need one. The range is the subject of "overlapped" and owns nothing, so "range's" leaves the verb without a subject.

D.why: You correctly wrote "colonies'," but then made "range" possessive too. The noun right before the verb "overlapped" doesn't own anything, so it can't take an apostrophe.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When the Harbor Point district was rezoned for mixed use in 2021, city planners held fourteen public hearings over eight months. Long before the first building permit was issued, the ______ had already reshaped the plan: a proposed six-story parking garage became a covered produce market after dozens of people living within two blocks of the site argued that the neighborhood needed food more than parking.
explanation: There are three nouns here. The district owns the residents, and there is only one district (Harbor Point), so it takes 's. The residents own the objections, and there were "dozens of people," so the owner is plural and ends in s: residents'. The objections are the subject of "had reshaped" and own nothing, so they take no apostrophe.

B.why: You left out every apostrophe, but two of the nouns are owners. The district has residents, and the residents have objections.

C.why: You got the district right but gave the objections a single owner. The passage says dozens of people objected, so the possessive has to be plural: residents'.

D.why: You made "districts'" plural even though the passage names only one district. You also put an apostrophe on "objection's," the noun right before the verb, which owns nothing.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The Osaka workshop of printmaker Kiyoe Tanabe, active in the 1870s, employed three carvers, each assigned a different section of every design. Cut from seasoned cherry wood and inked by hand, the ______ were then aligned using small notches at their corners, so that every color in the finished print landed exactly where Tanabe intended.
explanation: The opening phrase describes the blocks, and the blocks belong to the carvers. The workshop had three carvers, so the owner is plural and ends in s: carvers'. The blocks are the subject of "were aligned" and own nothing, so they are plain plural: blocks.

A.why: You were probably pulled in by "each assigned a different section" and treated the owner as singular. The blocks come from all three carvers, so you need the plural possessive carvers'.

C.why: You put the apostrophe on the wrong noun. The carvers own the blocks, but the blocks, the subject of "were aligned," don't own anything.

D.why: You got "carvers'" right but also made "block's" possessive. The last noun before the verb owns nothing, and "block's" is singular besides, which clashes with "were."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Few eighteenth-century maps of the southern Andes survive, and most of those that do were drawn in Lima from travelers' secondhand reports. One notable exception is the work of a single surveyor, Tomás Orrego, who crossed the cordillera alone in 1784 carrying a barometer and a compass. Historians now consider the ______ more reliable than the official maps of the period, because his elevations were measured on site rather than estimated.
explanation: The sketches belong to the surveyor. The passage says "a single surveyor" who crossed "alone," and the later "his" confirms there is one owner, so the possessive is surveyor's. The sketches are the object of "consider" and own nothing, so they take no apostrophe.

A.why: You left out the apostrophe that shows ownership. The surveyor owns the sketches, so he needs a possessive.

C.why: You used a plural owner, but the passage stresses that there is one surveyor working alone. A single owner takes 's, not s'.

D.why: You got the owner right but added an apostrophe to "sketch's." The sketches are an object and own nothing. They are only plural.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Labor economist Priya Venkataraman collected payroll records from 340 manufacturing plants scattered across rural and suburban counties to test whether nearby competition for workers raises pay. Her findings were striking. Across all of the plants she studied, the ______ earned, on average, 9 percent more when a competing employer operated within five kilometers, even after she adjusted for differences in local living costs and in the skill requirements of each job.
explanation: The employees belong to the plants. The sentence says "across all of the plants," which means 340 owners, so the possessive is plural: plants'. The employees are the subject of "earned" and own nothing, so they are plain plural with no apostrophe.

A.why: You switched the roles. The plants are the owners and need an apostrophe. The employees come right before the verb "earned" and own nothing.

B.why: You found the right owner but made it singular. The study covers 340 plants, and the sentence says "all of the plants," so you need plants'.

D.why: You used one plant when the passage names many, and you also added an apostrophe to "employee's," the noun before the verb, which owns nothing.
